transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because… well, it’s been about a year of this, and I know it sounds like a lot when I say it all at once. I work around labs, so I notice things, you know? Numbers, charts, when something doesn’t look right.

It’s about my dad’s lab results. I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing parts of them or holding them back. And everybody keeps telling me they’re fine—doctors, my family, everyone—but the chart doesn’t match what I saw. It just doesn’t. And I keep going over it and trying to explain it, and it’s wearing me down.

Aside from your concerns about your dad's lab results, have you noticed anything unusual with your senses—like hearing voices or sounds that others don't seem to hear, or seeing things that others don't see?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I hear normal things—like at work there’s always machines beeping, carts, people talking in the hall, and sometimes you think someone called your name but it’s just the noise, you know? But not voices like… talking to me or anything.

And I haven’t seen things that weren’t there. I’m pretty observant, maybe more than people like, because with blood draws you have to notice tiny things—labels, timing, whether something’s been spun down right—but that’s different. My eyes and ears are fine, as far as I can tell.
When you think about your dad's lab results being altered, is there any part of you that wonders if you might be mistaken, or are you completely certain that this is happening?

I mean… I’ve asked myself that, because everybody keeps saying I’m overthinking it. But no, not really. I know what I saw. The chart doesn’t match it.

And it’s not like I don’t understand labs—I work around this stuff, I know how numbers get entered, how things show up, when something is missing. My aunt once had a portal issue where half her records didn’t load for two days, so people act like systems are perfect but they’re not. Anyway, with my dad’s results, it’s been going on for about a year, and it feels like someone in the clinic system is changing things or holding parts back. Doctors and family keep telling me the numbers are fine, but they’re looking at the altered chart, not what I saw. So… I don’t think I’m mistaken.
Do you have any history of head injury, seizures, thyroid or other medical illnesses, or use of drugs, alcohol, or medications that could be affecting your thinking?

I don’t think there’s anything like that, no… I mean, nothing that jumps out to me as, “this would explain it,” if that’s what you mean.

I’m pretty careful about that kind of thing because in labs they’re always asking about medications or conditions before certain tests, and people forget to mention things all the time—like they’ll say “no meds” and then it turns out they take something every day, so I get why you’re asking. But for me, I’m not aware of anything medical or substance-related that would be messing with my thinking.

Outside of this concern about your dad's lab results, how are things going for you at work and in your relationships—are you able to function normally in those areas, or has this belief started to affect other parts of your life as well?

I mean, mostly I’m functioning. I still go to my phlebotomy shifts, I show up, I do the draws, I handle the labels and the patients and all of that. I pay my bills, keep my place together, shower, groceries—normal stuff.

It’s not like I’m just sitting in a room all day staring at the portal, even though people kind of act like that’s what I’m doing. And work is busy anyway, so you don’t really get to fall apart—you’ve got someone fasting since midnight, someone else who’s scared of needles, then the printer jams, and everyone blames the person at the front. So… yeah, outside of the issue with my dad’s records, I’m still managing my normal responsibilities.

Aside from the concern about your dad's lab results, have you had any other suspicions or beliefs—about other people, situations, or being watched or targeted in some way—that others might find hard to believe?

Not really like being watched or anything… I mean, people make everything sound dramatic when they repeat it back. It’s mainly this one thing with my dad’s lab results.

That’s why I’m here, because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove someone in the clinic system is changing things or holding parts back. And I know how that sounds, but I work around lab stuff, I know what a chart should look like. Like when results disappear or the timing doesn’t line up—people who don’t deal with it every day just think you’re confused, but I’m not.

My family keeps saying, “The doctors say he’s fine,” but they’re looking at the chart after it’s been changed. So no, it’s not like I think everyone is after me. It’s this specific thing, and it’s exhausting because nobody will take it seriously.

Over this past year, have you noticed any sustained changes in your mood—like periods of feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or low energy, or on the other end, unusually elevated, energetic, or needing much less sleep than usual?

I don’t know… I mean, not in some clear way that I can point to. I get tired, sure, but who doesn’t when you’re working and then trying to keep track of all this paperwork and calls and portal messages?

It’s hard to separate “mood” from just being worn down by people not listening. Like, if someone tells you over and over that you’re imagining something, of course you’re going to feel irritated or drained. But I wouldn’t say I’ve had, like, a separate period where I was suddenly a totally different person or anything.

The sleep thing is tricky too because sometimes I stay up later than I should, but that happens when you’re trying to find one specific thing and then the website times out, and then you remember you need laundry for work the next day. So… I’m not sure. I haven’t noticed some big mood swing, if that’s what you mean.

Have you noticed any changes in how you express yourself—like trouble organizing your thoughts, speaking in ways others find hard to follow, or losing interest in things you used to enjoy—beyond this specific concern about your dad's results?

I’m not sure. I don’t think I talk differently, but people act like I’m “going in circles” just because I’m trying to explain the sequence. And if you don’t start with the first portal entry, then the rest doesn’t make sense, you know? It’s like when we have a patient come in and they swear they drank water but not coffee, and then later they mention cream, and suddenly the whole fasting thing changes—details matter.

As far as interest in things… I mean, I still do things. Maybe not as much, but it’s also been a weird year. I’ll start watching something and then remember I meant to check a message, or I’ll be folding laundry and think about whether I saved a screenshot. But I don’t feel like I’ve become someone who can’t enjoy anything. I just… my mind goes back to it because it’s important.

If your father's doctor showed you the original, unedited lab records and lab technician logs proving nothing had been altered, do you think that would change your mind, or would you still believe the results had been tampered with?

I mean… if they showed me something, I’d look at it. I’m not refusing to look. But “original” is kind of the whole problem, you know? In a clinic system, things get entered, corrected, scanned, re-uploaded—there are access logs, timestamps, all these little places where something can look official after the fact.

So would it change my mind? I don’t think just someone handing me a printout and saying, “See, nothing happened,” would settle it. Because I know what I saw before, and the chart doesn’t match that. I’ve been trying for a year to prove someone changed something or held part of it back, and every time a doctor or my family says the numbers are fine, they’re basing it on what’s there now.

It’s like at work—if a tube is mislabeled, everyone wants to act like the computer is the truth, but the process matters. Who touched it, when it was released, whether something was corrected. So I’d need to see more than just “the records.” And honestly, even then… I’d be looking for where the gap is, because there is one. That’s the part that’s wearing me down.

opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a single, well-systematized, non-bizarre delusion (belief that a clinic system is altering/withholding her father's lab results) persisting for approximately one year, held with firm conviction despite reassurance and lack of evidence, and not amenable to alternative explanation even when presented with hypothetical disconfirming evidence. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech or thought disorder (her explanations are detailed and logically sequential, reflecting occupational familiarity with lab systems rather than looseness of association), no negative symptoms, and no mood episode of sufficient duration or severity to account for the delusion (she denies sustained depressive or manic symptoms, and mild fatigue/irritability is attributed to stress from the belief itself, not a primary mood disturbance). Functioning is well preserved (maintains job performance, self-care, and daily responsibilities) apart from the circumscribed impact of the delusional preoccupation. No medical, neurological, or substance-related etiology is identified. This pattern—one non-bizarre delusion, intact functioning, absence of other psychotic or mood symptoms—is most consistent with Delusional Disorder (F22), specifically a persecutory/jealous-type variant focused on a specific person (her father) and system (the clinic). Schizophrenia (F20.0) is less likely given absence of hallucinations, disorganization, or negative symptoms. Other specified psychotic disorder (F28) was considered but the presentation fits the specific criteria for delusional disorder better given the singular, systematized nature of the belief and preserved functioning.
